Systems biology has profited in various ways\r\nfrom machine learning techniques but in particular from network inference, i.e. the\r\nlearning of interactions given observed quantities of the involved components or data\r\nthat stem from interventional experiments. Originally this domain of system biology\r\nwas confined to the inference of gene regulation networks but recently expanded to other\r\nlevels of organization of biological and ecological systems. Especially the application to\r\nspecies interaction networks in a varying environment is of mounting importance in\r\norder to improve our understanding of the dynamics of species extinctions, invasions,\r\nand population behaviour in general.\r\nThe aim of this thesis is to demonstrate an extensive study of various state-of-art\r\nmachine learning techniques applied to a genetic regulation system in plants and to\r\nexpand and modify some of these methods to infer species interaction networks in an\r\necological setting. The first study attempts to improve the knowledge about circadian\r\nregulation in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana from the view point of machine learning and\r\ngives suggestions on what methods are best suited for inference, how the data should\r\nbe processed and modelled mathematically, and what quality of network learning can\r\nbe expected by doing so. To achieve this, I generate a rich and realistic synthetic data\r\nset that is used for various studies under consideration of different effects and method\r\nsetups. The best method and setup is applied to real transcriptional data, which leads\r\nto a new hypothesis about the circadian clock network structure.\r\nThe ecological study is focused on the development of two novel inference methods\r\nthat exploit a common principle from transcriptional time-series, which states that expression\r\nprofiles over time can be temporally heterogeneous. A corresponding concept\r\nin a spatial domain of 2 dimensions is that species interaction dynamics can be spatially\r\nheterogeneous, i.e. can change in space dependent on the environment and other\r\nfactors. I will demonstrate the expansion from the 1-dimensional time domain to the\r\n2-dimensional spatial domain, introduce two distinct space segmentation schemes, and\r\nconsider species dispersion effects with spatial autocorrelation. The two novel methods\r\ndisplay a significant improvement in species interaction inference compared to competing\r\nmethods and display a high confidence in learning the spatial structure of different\r\nspecies neighbourhoods or environments","documentType":"thesis","doi":null,"downloadUrl":"https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/download\/30319422.pdf","fieldOfStudy":null,"id":388398854,"identifiers":[{"identifier":"30319422","type":"core_id"},{"identifier":"oai:research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk:10023\/7030","type":"oai_id"},{"identifier":"oai:research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk:10023\/7030","type":"oai"}],"title":"Machine learning in systems biology at different scales : from molecular biology to ecology","language":{"code":"en","name":"English"},"magId":null,"oaiIds":["oai:research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk:10023\/7030"],"publishedDate":"","publisher":"The University of St Andrews","pubmedId":null,"references":[{"id":"54869832","title":"A Bayesian approach to reconstructing genetic regulatory networks with hidden factors.","authors":[],"date":"2005","doi":null,"raw":"Beal, M. Probabilistic machine learning is valuable in these settings, as it quantifies predictive uncertainty, notably by generating probabilistic predictions. We focus on regression, where the goal is to predict one or more continuous outputs given a set of inputs. In this context, we consider two main forms of uncertainty representation: predictive distributions, which assign probabilities to possible output values, and prediction sets, which are designed to contain the true output with a pre-specified probability. For these predictions to be reliable and informative, they must be calibrated and sharp, i.e., statistically consistent with observed data and concentrated around the true value.\r\n\r\nIn this thesis, we develop distribution-free regression methods to produce calibrated and sharp probabilistic predictions using neural network models. We consider both single-output and the less-explored multi-output regression settings. Specifically, we develop and study recalibration, regularization, and conformal prediction (CP) methods. The first adjusts predictions after model training, the second augments the training objective, and the last produces prediction sets with finite-sample coverage guarantees.\r\n\r\nFor single-output regression, we conduct a large-scale experimental study to provide a comprehensive comparison of these methods. The results reveal that post-hoc approaches consistently achieve superior calibration. We explain this finding by establishing a formal link between recalibration and CP, showing that recalibration also benefits from finite-sample coverage guarantees. However, the separate training and recalibration steps typically lead to degraded negative log-likelihood. To address this issue, we develop an end-to-end training procedure that incorporates the recalibration objective directly into learning, resulting in improved negative log-likelihood while maintaining calibration.\r\n\r\nFor multi-output regression, we conduct a comparative study of CP methods and introduce new classes of approaches that offer novel trade-offs between sharpness, compatibility with generative models, and computational efficiency. A key challenge in CP is achieving conditional coverage, which ensures that coverage guarantees hold for specific inputs rather than only on average. To address this, we propose a method that improves conditional coverage using conditional quantile regression, thereby avoiding the need to estimate full conditional distributions. Finally, for tasks requiring a full predictive density, we introduce a recalibration technique that operates in the latent space of invertible generative models such as conditional normalizing flows. This approach yields an explicit, calibrated multivariate probability density function. Collectively, these contributions advance the theory and practice of uncertainty quantification in machine learning, facilitating the development of more reliable predictive systems across diverse applications","documentType":"thesis","doi":null,"downloadUrl":"https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/download\/698103692.pdf","fieldOfStudy":null,"id":396932248,"identifiers":[{"identifier":"698103692","type":"core_id"},{"identifier":"oai:orbi.umons.ac.be:20.500.12907\/54123","type":"oai_id"},{"identifier":"oai:orbi.umons.ac.be:20.500.12907\/54123","type":"oai"}],"title":"Distribution-Free and Calibrated Predictive Uncertainty in Probabilistic Machine Learning","language":null,"magId":null,"oaiIds":["oai:orbi.umons.ac.be:20.500.12907\/54123"],"publishedDate":"2025-01-01T00:00:00+00:00","publisher":"UMONS - University of Mons","pubmedId":null,"references":[],"sourceFulltextUrls":["https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/download\/698103692.pdf"],"updatedDate":"2026-08-26T13:03:58+01:00","yearPublished":2025,"journals":[],"links":[{"type":"download","url":"https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/download\/698103692.pdf"},{"type":"reader","url":"https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/reader\/698103692"},{"type":"thumbnail_m","url":"https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/image\/698103692\/large"},{"type":"thumbnail_l","url":"https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/image\/698103692\/large"},{"type":"display","url":"https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/works\/396932248"}]},{"acceptedDate":"","arxivId":null,"authors":[{"name":"Aderhold, Andrej"}],"citationCount":0,"contributors":["Smith, Victoria Anne","Husmeier, Dirk"],"outputs":["https:\/\/api.core.ac.uk\/v3\/outputs\/30319422"],"createdDate":"2016-02-01T14:20:40+00:00","dataProviders":[{"id":95,"name":"St Andrews Research Repository","url":"https:\/\/api.core.ac.uk\/v3\/data-providers\/95","logo":"https:\/\/api.core.ac.uk\/data-providers\/95\/logo"}],"depositedDate":"2016-03-28T01:00:00+01:00","abstract":"Machine learning has been a source for continuous methodological advances in the field of computational learning from data. Systems biology has profited in various ways\r\nfrom machine learning techniques but in particular from network inference, i.e. the\r\nlearning of interactions given observed quantities of the involved components or data\r\nthat stem from interventional experiments. Originally this domain of system biology\r\nwas confined to the inference of gene regulation networks but recently expanded to other\r\nlevels of organization of biological and ecological systems. Especially the application to\r\nspecies interaction networks in a varying environment is of mounting importance in\r\norder to improve our understanding of the dynamics of species extinctions, invasions,\r\nand population behaviour in general.\r\nThe aim of this thesis is to demonstrate an extensive study of various state-of-art\r\nmachine learning techniques applied to a genetic regulation system in plants and to\r\nexpand and modify some of these methods to infer species interaction networks in an\r\necological setting. The first study attempts to improve the knowledge about circadian\r\nregulation in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana from the view point of machine learning and\r\ngives suggestions on what methods are best suited for inference, how the data should\r\nbe processed and modelled mathematically, and what quality of network learning can\r\nbe expected by doing so. To achieve this, I generate a rich and realistic synthetic data\r\nset that is used for various studies under consideration of different effects and method\r\nsetups. The best method and setup is applied to real transcriptional data, which leads\r\nto a new hypothesis about the circadian clock network structure.\r\nThe ecological study is focused on the development of two novel inference methods\r\nthat exploit a common principle from transcriptional time-series, which states that expression\r\nprofiles over time can be temporally heterogeneous. A corresponding concept\r\nin a spatial domain of 2 dimensions is that species interaction dynamics can be spatially\r\nheterogeneous, i.e. can change in space dependent on the environment and other\r\nfactors. I will demonstrate the expansion from the 1-dimensional time domain to the\r\n2-dimensional spatial domain, introduce two distinct space segmentation schemes, and\r\nconsider species dispersion effects with spatial autocorrelation. The two novel methods\r\ndisplay a significant improvement in species interaction inference compared to competing\r\nmethods and display a high confidence in learning the spatial structure of different\r\nspecies neighbourhoods or environments","documentType":"thesis","doi":null,"downloadUrl":"https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/download\/30319422.pdf","fieldOfStudy":null,"id":333776557,"identifiers":[{"identifier":"30319422","type":"core_id"},{"identifier":"oai:research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk:10023\/7030","type":"oai_id"},{"identifier":"oai:research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk:10023\/7030","type":"oai"}],"title":"Machine learning in systems biology at different scales : from molecular biology to ecology","language":{"code":"en","name":"English"},"magId":null,"oaiIds":["oai:research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk:10023\/7030"],"publishedDate":"","publisher":"The University of St Andrews","pubmedId":null,"references":[{"id":"49731770","title":"A Bayesian approach to reconstructing genetic regulatory networks with hidden factors.","authors":[],"date":"2005","doi":null,"raw":"Beal, M. Yet the vocal modality is under-exploited as a controller\r\nfor music systems. If we can analyse a vocal performance suitably in real time,\r\nthen this information could be used to create voice-based interfaces with the\r\npotential for intuitive and ful lling levels of expressive control.\r\nConversely, many modern techniques for music synthesis do not imply any\r\nparticular interface. Should a given parameter be controlled via a MIDI keyboard,\r\nor a slider\/fader, or a rotary dial? Automatic vocal analysis could provide\r\na fruitful basis for expressive interfaces to such electronic musical instruments.\r\nThe principal questions in applying vocal-based control are how to extract\r\nmusically meaningful information from the voice signal in real time, and how\r\nto convert that information suitably into control data. In this thesis we address\r\nthese questions, with a focus on timbral control, and in particular we\r\ndevelop approaches that can be used with a wide variety of musical instruments\r\nby applying machine learning techniques to automatically derive the mappings\r\nbetween expressive audio input and control output. The vocal audio signal is\r\nconstrued to include a broad range of expression, in particular encompassing\r\nthe extended techniques used in human beatboxing.\r\nThe central contribution of this work is the application of supervised and\r\nunsupervised machine learning techniques to automatically map vocal timbre\r\nto synthesiser timbre and controls. Component contributions include a delayed\r\ndecision-making strategy for low-latency sound classi cation, a regression-tree\r\nmethod to learn associations between regions of two unlabelled datasets, a fast\r\nestimator of multidimensional di erential entropy and a qualitative method for\r\nevaluating musical interfaces based on discourse analysis","documentType":"thesis","doi":null,"downloadUrl":"https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/download\/30695107.pdf","fieldOfStudy":null,"id":390445633,"identifiers":[{"identifier":"30695107","type":"core_id"},{"identifier":"oai:qmro.qmul.ac.uk:123456789\/412","type":"oai_id"},{"identifier":"oai:qmro.qmul.ac.uk:123456789\/412","type":"oai"}],"title":"Making music through real-time voice timbre analysis: machine learning and timbral control","language":{"code":"en","name":"English"},"magId":null,"oaiIds":["oai:qmro.qmul.ac.uk:123456789\/412"],"publishedDate":"2010-01-01T00:00:00+00:00","publisher":"Queen Mary University of London","pubmedId":null,"references":[{"id":"55048091","title":"A comparison of the reproducibility and the sensitivity to change of visual analogue scales, Borg scales, and Likert scales in normal subjects during submaximal exercise.","authors":[],"date":"1999","doi":null,"raw":"S. Yet the vocal modality is under-exploited as a controller\r\nfor music systems. If we can analyse a vocal performance suitably in real time,\r\nthen this information could be used to create voice-based interfaces with the\r\npotential for intuitive and ful lling levels of expressive control.\r\nConversely, many modern techniques for music synthesis do not imply any\r\nparticular interface. Should a given parameter be controlled via a MIDI keyboard,\r\nor a slider\/fader, or a rotary dial? Automatic vocal analysis could provide\r\na fruitful basis for expressive interfaces to such electronic musical instruments.\r\nThe principal questions in applying vocal-based control are how to extract\r\nmusically meaningful information from the voice signal in real time, and how\r\nto convert that information suitably into control data. Yet the vocal modality is under-exploited as a controller\r\nfor music systems. If we can analyse a vocal performance suitably in real time,\r\nthen this information could be used to create voice-based interfaces with the\r\npotential for intuitive and ful lling levels of expressive control.\r\nConversely, many modern techniques for music synthesis do not imply any\r\nparticular interface. Should a given parameter be controlled via a MIDI keyboard,\r\nor a slider\/fader, or a rotary dial? Automatic vocal analysis could provide\r\na fruitful basis for expressive interfaces to such electronic musical instruments.\r\nThe principal questions in applying vocal-based control are how to extract\r\nmusically meaningful information from the voice signal in real time, and how\r\nto convert that information suitably into control data. In this thesis we address\r\nthese questions, with a focus on timbral control, and in particular we\r\ndevelop approaches that can be used with a wide variety of musical instruments\r\nby applying machine learning techniques to automatically derive the mappings\r\nbetween expressive audio input and control output. The vocal audio signal is\r\nconstrued to include a broad range of expression, in particular encompassing\r\nthe extended techniques used in human beatboxing.\r\nThe central contribution of this work is the application of supervised and\r\nunsupervised machine learning techniques to automatically map vocal timbre\r\nto synthesiser timbre and controls. Component contributions include a delayed\r\ndecision-making strategy for low-latency sound classi cation, a regression-tree\r\nmethod to learn associations between regions of two unlabelled datasets, a fast\r\nestimator of multidimensional di erential entropy and a qualitative method for\r\nevaluating musical interfaces based on discourse analysis","documentType":"thesis","doi":null,"downloadUrl":"https:\/\/core.ac.uk\/download\/30695107.pdf","fieldOfStudy":null,"id":384955760,"identifiers":[{"identifier":"30695107","type":"core_id"},{"identifier":"oai:qmro.qmul.ac.uk:123456789\/412","type":"oai_id"},{"identifier":"oai:qmro.qmul.ac.uk:123456789\/412","type":"oai"}],"title":"Making music through real-time voice timbre analysis: machine learning and timbral control","language":{"code":"en","name":"English"},"magId":null,"oaiIds":["oai:qmro.qmul.ac.uk:123456789\/412"],"publishedDate":"2010-01-01T00:00:00+00:00","publisher":"Queen Mary University of London","pubmedId":null,"references":[{"id":"53679787","title":"A comparison of the reproducibility and the sensitivity to change of visual analogue scales, Borg scales, and Likert scales in normal subjects during submaximal exercise.","authors":[],"date":"1999","doi":null,"raw":"S.
